title: Probing Deconfined Quantum Criticality Point on a Digital Quantum Computer
abstract: A deconfined quantum critical point (DQCP) is a continuous transition between ordered phases with unrelated broken symmetries, beyond the Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson paradigm. In one dimension, such a transition between a $z$-polarized ferromagnet (zFM) and a valence-bond solid (VBS) is well established numerically in a frustrated spin-$1/2$ chain. Here we ask whether a superconducting quantum processor can resolve this transition and its signatures despite finite-size effects and device noise. The ground states are prepared by ancilla-projected quantum imaginary-time evolution (QITE), whose exact target states are compressed by tensor-network optimization into shallow depth quantum circuits. The hardware data distinguish the phases through their order parameters, spin and dimer correlations, structure factors, correlation ratios, and snapshot distributions. The crossing of the order parameters locates the transition, and its finite-size extrapolation lies close to the thermodynamic-limit value obtained from large-scale numerics. A noise model based on the device calibration accounts quantitatively for the reduced amplitudes measured on hardware. Our findings demonstrate that a Landau-forbidden transition between competing orders can be resolved on current quantum processors.
summary: This paper uses a superconducting quantum computer to simulate a quantum phase transition—the Deconfined Quantum Critical Point—in a 1D spin chain. By employing advanced techniques like ancilla-projected QITE and developing a detailed noise model, the authors successfully resolve the transition point despite hardware noise and finite-size effects. This demonstrates a significant capability for quantum computation in simulating complex strongly correlated quantum matter.
main_problem: The paper aims to determine if a superconducting quantum processor can successfully resolve the signatures of a Deconfined Quantum Critical Point (DQCP) transition, which occurs between unrelated ordered phases.
main_result: The study successfully demonstrates that a Landau-forbidden transition between a zFM and VBS order can be resolved on current quantum processors, with results agreeing with large-scale numerics.
method: The methodology combines quantum simulation using Ancilla-projected Quantum Imaginary-Time Evolution (QITE) mapped onto shallow quantum circuits, alongside rigorous noise modeling and finite-size extrapolation.
model_or_system: The system is a one-dimensional spin-1/2 chain governed by a Hamiltonian involving nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor interactions, exhibiting competition between a zFM phase and a Valence Bond Solid (VBS) phase.
key_observables: Order parameters ($M_{FM}^z$, $\Psi_{VBS}$), spin and dimer correlations, structure factors, and correlation ratios.
important_parameters: Frustration strength ($K$), system size ($L$), and applied magnetic/dimerization fields ($h_z, h_d$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a noise model calibrated against device measurements, and the ability to compress the QITE process into shallow quantum circuits.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the zFM $	o$ VBS transition crossing, the workflow mapping QITE to PQC ansatz, and the determination of the noise scale ($\lambda$) by fitting measured observables to theoretical models.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical model and the goal of probing the DQCP. It details the quantum circuit implementation (QITE $	o$ PQC) and measurement techniques. Subsequently, it focuses heavily on characterizing and mitigating device noise using density matrix formalism and fitting procedures. Finally, it presents the results showing the successful resolution of the transition point.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges the gap between highly complex, strongly correlated theoretical models (like DQCPs) and the practical limitations of near-term quantum hardware, providing a roadmap for quantum simulation in condensed matter physics.
